summary: This RFC identifies the documents specifying the official protocols used in the Internet, and is an official status report for the ARPA Internet community. It replaced earlier editions and was itself replaced by RFC 944.

eli5.summary: A regularly updated list of official network rulebooks. This edition was soon replaced by a newer one.

questions: what were the official internet protocols in 1984
status report on arpa internet protocols
what is the difference between required recommended and experimental protocols
subtitle: The official Internet protocols catalog for 1984.

tldr.problem: The Internet community needed an authoritative list of which protocols were official, their status, and implementation guidance.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC identifies and documents each official protocol with its status (required, recommended, elective, or experimental), specification, and known issues.
tldr.outcome: It served as the official status report for ARPA-Internet protocols in 1984 and was replaced the following year by RFC 944.

today: RFC 924 is Historic. It was superseded by RFC 944 in April 1985, which provided an updated protocol status report. Modern protocol status is tracked through the IETF standards track and IANA registries.

sections.title: Introduction and Purpose
sections.content:
RFC 924 identifies the documents that specify the official protocols used in the Internet and is an official status report on protocols in the ARPA-Internet community. The RFC organizes protocols into categories with notes on status, specification documents, comments on implementation, other references, dependencies, and contact people.

The RFC notes that the foundation of official protocols comes from the "Internet Protocol Transition Workbook" (IPTW) dated March 1982. Some protocols have been revised since then into specialized volumes like the "Internet Mail Protocols" and "Internet Telnet Protocol and Options."
sections.eli5: This document lists which network rules the Internet officially uses. It says who wrote each rule, what problems were found, and who to ask questions about it.

sections.title: Organization and Status Levels
sections.content:
Each protocol entry includes the same fields: STATUS, SPECIFICATION, COMMENTS, OTHER REFERENCES, DEPENDENCIES, and CONTACT. The status indicates how essential each protocol is:

  • Required: all hosts must implement this protocol
  • Recommended: all hosts are encouraged to implement this protocol
  • Elective: hosts may implement or not, at their discretion
  • Experimental: hosts should not implement unless participating in the experiment and coordinated with the contact

The RFC is organized into sections covering overview information, network level protocols, host level protocols, application level protocols, and support protocols.
sections.eli5: Every protocol gets a label: Required means everyone must use it, Recommended means try to use it, Elective means it is optional, and Experimental means do not use it unless you are trying it out.

sections.title: Network and Core Protocols
sections.content:
Internet Protocol (IP), specified in RFC 791, is the required universal protocol of the Internet. It provides datagram service with universal host addressing. The RFC notes minor issues in the specification, particularly in route option processing.

Internet Control Message Protocol (ICMP), specified in RFC 792, provides control messages and error reports for IP. It is integral to IP; a complete IP implementation must include ICMP. The RFC notes that additional ICMP message types for addressing have been proposed.

At the gateway level, the Exterior Gateway Protocol (EGP) is recommended for exchanging routing information between gateways of different administrations. Experimental gateway protocols like the Gateway Gateway Protocol (GGP) are used in core gateways.
sections.eli5: IP is the main rule that delivers messages between computers on the Internet. ICMP is the error-reporting system that tells you when something goes wrong. Gateway protocols help routers talk to each other.

sections.title: Host-Level Transport Protocols
sections.content:
User Datagram Protocol (UDP), specified in RFC 768, is recommended. It provides datagram service to applications by adding port addressing to IP. The RFC notes that a minor clarification was made regarding checksum computation.

Transmission Control Protocol (TCP), specified in RFC 793, is recommended and provides reliable end-to-end data stream service. The RFC acknowledges many corrections and clarifications needed in the specification, including issues with event processing, the push mechanism, urgent data handling, and maximum segment size behavior.

Other experimental host protocols include the Host Monitoring Protocol (HMP) for debugging, various experimental protocols like Stream Protocol (ST) for real-time applications, and Reliable Data Protocol (RDP) for bulk data transfer in environments with long delays.
sections.eli5: UDP is the quick way to send messages with no promises about delivery. TCP is the reliable way to send data that must arrive complete. Different experimental protocols do specialized jobs like monitoring computers or handling voice.

sections.title: Application Protocols
sections.content:
Telnet Protocol, specified in RFC 854, is recommended for remote terminal access and has been revised since the earlier IPTW documentation. The RFC references the "Internet Telnet Protocol and Options" volume which contains the Telnet protocol definition and a comprehensive list of option types.

Simple Mail Transfer Protocol (SMTP) and related mail protocols are covered in the "Internet Mail Protocols" volume. File Transfer Protocol (FTP) and Domain Name System (DNS) are also listed as official protocols.

The RFC also mentions experimental protocols for specialized use cases, including Network Voice Protocol (NVP-II) for real-time voice conferencing.
sections.eli5: Telnet lets you control a distant computer as if you were sitting at it. Email protocols send mail over the Internet. FTP moves files between computers.
